agent_explanations_oldest_first.text: That search matched itself (block 153). The earlier computation of each head's output for the mean end-of-prompt state was block 147, so I print its relevant lines. That fixes the layer index and normalisation convention for V_last before I build anything. I also check the shapes of the stored generation activations: residuals at the last prompt token and averaged over answer tokens, from pass 1 of the original model.

My earlier block 147 read the residual at index 10 as the input to L11. In this tool's convention (0 = embeddings, l = after layer l, 27 entries), the input to `model.layers.11` is index 11, so those numbers were one layer early. The conclusions were drawn only from summary statistics and the edits themselves were measured in real passes, so nothing tested is affected, but I use index 11 from now on.

I recompute the mean value vectors at the true L11 input (with the input-norm scale folded in), for the last prompt token (V_last) and for the mean answer state (V_ans). From them I get:
- their norms and how aligned they are;
- each head's write of V_last;
- the share of head 3's weights that T1 would remove.

T1 projects the V_last direction out of head 3's output columns on the value side. It is a rank-1 edit on 256 columns: head 3 then no longer writes the content it retrieves from the end-of-prompt token, but keeps everything else it does.

If T1 matches ×0.2 (about +18), the harm is specifically head 3's broadcast of the end-of-prompt state. If it does little, the harm lies in what head 3 retrieves elsewhere, and whole-head damping remains the edit. I save T1 and log it for the next pass.

The end-of-prompt value vector is very large: |V_last| = 16.1, against 2.2 for the mean answer-token value (cos 0.35). With about a quarter of heads 2 and 3's answer-time attention landing on that token, it dominates what they retrieve.

Head 3 is the outlier in how strongly it passes this vector on. Its gain along the V_last direction is 1.37, above its own average gain (0.995). Every sibling responds below its own average (0.59/0.68, 0.29/0.47, 0.41/0.62). As a result, head 3 writes 22.0 for V_last, against 4.7–9.5 for the others.

That is the signature I would expect from a brake built into head 3's output matrix: an extra response tuned to the end-of-prompt broadcast. T1 removes exactly this response, a rank-1 change carrying only 0.7% of head 3's weight energy, and leaves the rest of the head intact.

I now run T1 paired on DEV[1024:1250] (whole-head ×0.2 gave +18.6 there).
- If T1 recovers most of that gain, the brake is head 3's broadcast of the end-of-prompt state, and T1 is a far more targeted undo.
- If it gives little, the harm is spread over head 3's normal retrieval, and whole-head damping stays the edit.

This is the brake, located precisely. T1 removes only head 3's response to the end-of-prompt value direction: a rank-1 change carrying 0.7% of that head's weight energy. It gives +25.7 ± 3.4 points (66 wrong→right, only 8 right→wrong). Accuracy rises from 18.6% to 44.2%, cut-offs fall from 28% to 7%, and mean answer length from 346 to 247 tokens.

That is clearly better than damping the whole head (×0.2: +18.6) on the same problems. So the harm is not head 3 as such but its amplified pass-through of the large end-of-prompt value vector to every answer token, and the head's other, useful function is now kept.

Next I make the edit clean, check whether there are more brakes of the same kind, and understand what it removes:

1. **DEV-only direction.** The V_last direction came from the pass-1 activations. If pass 1 included HOLDOUT problems, I rebuild the direction from DEV problems only, so that HOLDOUT stays untouched.
2. **What the removed write does.** I characterise head 3's write along that input direction: its size, its massive-dimension share, its alignment with the spike and with D1, its effect after the post-norm, and a logit lens on a few curated tokens.
3. **Same anomaly elsewhere.** I scan all 104 heads for a gain on their own layer's end-of-prompt value direction that is unusually high relative to the head's average gain. In L11 the siblings sit at 0.6–0.9× and head 3 at 1.37×. A planted brake of the same kind elsewhere would show up as a similar outlier.
